_comment: Eastern Cape Department of Education Grade 11 Physical Sciences P2 (Chemistry), November 2025 provincial common examination.
Questions and marking-guideline answers extracted from the text layer of the official PDFs
(paper2.pdf, paper2_memo.pdf) and read against the rendered pages. The guideline is
bilingual (English/Afrikaans); only the English is transcribed. memo_answer gives the guideline's
working and final answers (tick marks removed); diagrams, graphs and circuits are described in
brackets in the question text. Data sheets printed with the paper are not transcribed.
FORMAT: 150 marks, 3 hours, nine compulsory questions (Q1 multiple choice 20 marks).

questions.context: QUESTION 1: MULTIPLE-CHOICE QUESTIONS. Various options are provided as possible answers to the following questions. Choose the answer and write only the letter (A-D) next to the question numbers (1.1 to 1.10) in the ANSWER BOOK, for example 1.11 E.
questions.text: Which ONE of the following molecules contains a dative covalent bond? A H2O B NH3 C BF3 D NH4+
questions.topic: Atomic combinations: bonding, molecular shapes and polarity
questions.memo_answer: D

questions.text: Consider the chemical bonds shown below: C-C, C=C, C≡C. Which ONE of the following combinations regarding the bond length and bond energy is CORRECT? (SHORTEST BOND LENGTH | HIGHEST BOND ENERGY) A C-C | C-C; B C=C | C=C; C C≡C | C≡C; D C-C | C≡C
questions.topic: Atomic combinations: bonding, molecular shapes and polarity
questions.memo_answer: C

questions.text: Which ONE of the following substances have ION DIPOLE FORCES between its molecules? A H2O (ℓ) B CO2 (g) C NaCℓ (aq) D NaCℓ (s)
questions.memo_answer: C

questions.text: The diagram below shows a gas syringe containing a certain gas. When the plunger is at position A the volume occupied by the gas is X and exerts a pressure P. When the plunger moves to position B the volume occupied by the gas is ⅓X. [Diagram: gas syringe with the plunger at A (volume X, pressure P) and at B (volume ⅓X).] What is the DIFFERENCE in pressure exerted by the gas between points A and B? A 3P B ⅔P C ⅓P D 2P
questions.topic: Ideal gases and the gas laws
questions.memo_answer: D

questions.text: Consider the following statement regarding the activated complex during a chemical reaction: (I) The activation energy must be overcome to reach the activated complex. (II) It is the unstable transition state from reactants to products. (III) It is the energy released or absorbed during a chemical reaction. Which of the above statement(s) is/are CORRECT about the activated complex? A II and III only B II only C I and II only D I only
questions.memo_answer: C

questions.text: Consider the balanced equation: Na2CO3 (aq) + 2 HCℓ (aq) → 2 NaCℓ (aq) + H2O (ℓ) + CO2 (g). 1 mol of Na2CO3 reacts with 1 mol of HCℓ to yield 0,2 mol of CO2. Which ONE of the following combinations is CORRECT regarding the reaction? (Limiting reagent | % yield of CO2) A Na2CO3 | 40%; B Na2CO3 | 20%; C HCℓ | 40%; D HCℓ | 20%
questions.topic: Quantitative aspects: stoichiometry, limiting reagents and purity
questions.memo_answer: C

questions.text: Consider the incomplete equation below: H2Y + 2 NaOH → Na2Y + 2 H2O The formula of Y is … A Cℓ – B SO42– C NO3– D PO43–
questions.memo_answer: B

questions.text: Consider the following equation: (COOH)2 (aq) + H2O (ℓ) ⇌ (COO)22– (aq) + H3O+ (aq) The bases in the above reaction are … A (COOH)2 and H2O B (COO)22– and H3O+ C H2O and (COO)22– D (COOH)2 and (COO)22–
questions.memo_answer: C

questions.text: Consider the reaction below: 5 Zn + 2 MnO4– + 16 H+ → 5 Zn2+ + 2 Mn2+ + 8 H2O The reducing agent in the above reaction is … A Zn B MnO4– C H+ D Mn2+
questions.memo_answer: A

questions.text: How many electrons are needed to reduce 2 mol of H2O to 2 mol of OH⁻ and 1 mol of H2? A 2 B 3 C 4 D 5
questions.memo_answer: A

questions.context: QUESTION 2 (Start on a new page.) Consider the following substances (A-D) in the table below: A HOCℓ; B NF3; C H2S; D HCN.
questions.text: Define the term chemical bond.
questions.topic: Atomic combinations: bonding, molecular shapes and polarity
questions.memo_answer: A chemical bond is a mutual attraction between two atoms resulting from the simultaneous attraction between their nuclei and the outer electrons.

questions.context: 2.2 Draw the Lewis structures for the following molecules.
questions.text: HOCℓ
questions.topic: Atomic combinations: bonding, molecular shapes and polarity
questions.memo_answer: Lewis structure H:O:Cℓ - H shares one electron pair with O; O shares one electron pair with Cℓ; O has two lone pairs and Cℓ three lone pairs.

questions.text: HCN
questions.topic: Atomic combinations: bonding, molecular shapes and polarity
questions.memo_answer: Lewis structure H:C:::N - H shares one electron pair with C; C shares three electron pairs with N (triple bond); N has one lone pair.

questions.context: 2.3 Write down the name of the molecular shape for:
questions.text: H2S
questions.topic: Atomic combinations: bonding, molecular shapes and polarity
questions.memo_answer: Bent/ Angular

questions.text: NF3
questions.topic: Atomic combinations: bonding, molecular shapes and polarity
questions.memo_answer: Trigonal – pyramidal

questions.text: Is NF3 a POLAR or NON-POLAR molecule? Fully explain the answer.
questions.topic: Atomic combinations: bonding, molecular shapes and polarity
questions.memo_answer:
Polar.
• F is more electronegative than N / F attracts the bond electrons more towards itself / ΔEN = 4,0 - 3,0 = 1
• The N-F bond is polar
• The NF3 molecular geometry is asymmetrical.

questions.context: 2.5 Two hydrogen atoms form a bond according to the energy profile graph shown below. [Graph of potential energy (kJ·mol⁻¹) against distance (pm): A - two separate H atoms far apart (zero energy); the curve dips to a minimum; B - the depth of the minimum below zero (dashed arrow); C - the distance where the curve crosses zero; D - the steep part of the curve at very short distance where the atoms overlap strongly.] Use the letters A, B, C or D as it appears on the graph above to identify the following:
questions.text: Bond energy
questions.topic: Atomic combinations: bonding, molecular shapes and polarity
questions.memo_answer: B

questions.text: Point when repulsive forces are stronger than the attractive forces
questions.topic: Atomic combinations: bonding, molecular shapes and polarity
questions.memo_answer: D

questions.text: Explain the formation of H2 from the graph. Refer to the electrostatic force between the protons and electrons and energy involved.
questions.topic: Atomic combinations: bonding, molecular shapes and polarity
questions.memo_answer:
• As the two H atoms approaches each other, the electrons of the one H atom is attracted to the nucleus (protons) of the other H atom. The protons repel and electrons repel from the two H atoms.
• Attractive forces are greater than the repulsive forces, therefore the potential energy of the system decreases until it reaches the minimum value (most stable state)

questions.context: QUESTION 3 (Start on a new page.) 3.1 The diagram below is used to demonstrate the differences between intermolecular forces and intramolecular forces (chemical bonds) between two NH3 molecules. [Diagram: two NH3 molecules; (a) labels an N-H bond within a molecule; (b) labels the attraction between an H atom of one molecule and the N atom of the other.]
questions.text: Write down the name of the predominant intermolecular force that is represented by letter (b) in the diagram above.
questions.memo_answer: Hydrogen bond

questions.text: Write down TWO requirements for the formation of the force named in QUESTION 3.1.1.
questions.memo_answer:
• A hydrogen atom covalently bonded to a highly electronegative atom.
• A lone pair of electrons on a nearby highly electronegative atom.

questions.text: Write down the name of bond labelled (a).
questions.topic: Atomic combinations: bonding, molecular shapes and polarity
questions.memo_answer: (Polar) covalent bond

questions.text: Which ONE (a or b) requires the highest amount of energy to break/overcome its forces?
questions.memo_answer: a

questions.context: 3.2 Consider the boiling points of the hydrogen halides on group 16 as shown on the table below. [A H2S -60 °C; B H2Se -41 °C; C H2Te -2 °C]
questions.text: Define the term boiling point.
questions.memo_answer: The temperature at which the vapour pressure of a substance equals the atmospheric pressure

questions.text: Write down the phase of the hydrogen halides at room temperature.
questions.memo_answer: Gas

questions.text: Explain the trend observed in the boiling points of the hydrogen halides by referring to the molecular size and energy involved.
questions.memo_answer:
Marking criteria: state the increase in molecular size from H2S to H2Te; state the relationship between molecular size and London forces correctly; refer to the energy involved.
• From H2S to H2Te the molecular size increases.
• As the molecular size increases so does the strength of the London forces.
• More energy is needed to overcome the intermolecular forces from H2S to H2Te.

questions.text: Which hydrogen halide (H2S, H2Se or H2Te) will have the lowest vapour pressure at a certain temperature? Give a reason for the answer.
questions.memo_answer:
H2Te
It has the highest boiling point.

questions.text: How will the boiling point of HF compare to that of H2S? Choose from HIGHER THAN, LOWER THAN or EQUAL TO.
questions.memo_answer: HIGHER THAN

questions.text: Explain the answer in QUESTION 3.2.5 by referring to type of intermolecular forces and energy involved.
questions.memo_answer:
Marking criteria: state the dipole-dipole forces in H2S; state the hydrogen bonds in HF; compare the strength of the intermolecular forces; refer to the energy involved.
• HF has hydrogen bonds.
• H2S has dipole-dipole forces.
• Hydrogen bonds are stronger than dipole-dipole forces.
• More energy is needed to overcome the intermolecular forces in HF.
OR
• HF has hydrogen bonds; H2S has dipole-dipole forces; dipole-dipole forces are weaker than hydrogen bonds; less energy is needed to overcome the intermolecular forces in H2S.

questions.context: QUESTION 4 (Start on a new page.) A group of learners investigated the relationship between the pressure and volume of a certain gas. The graph of the pressure versus inverse of volume was obtained from the data in the investigation. [Graph: pressure (kPa, 0-140) against 1/volume (x 10⁻¹ cm⁻³, 0-1,15); a straight line through the origin with plotted points near 0,66 (96 kPa) to 0,88 (about 132 kPa).]
questions.text: Name the gas law that is investigated.
questions.topic: Ideal gases and the gas laws
questions.memo_answer: Boyle’s law

questions.context: 4.2 From the investigation write down:
questions.text: An investigative question for this investigation
questions.topic: Ideal gases and the gas laws
questions.memo_answer:
Criteria: the independent and dependent variables are stated; ask a question about the relationship between the independent and dependent variables.
How does the pressure of a gas affect the volume?
OR What is the relationship between pressure and volume of the gas?

questions.text: TWO controlled variables for this investigation
questions.topic: Ideal gases and the gas laws
questions.memo_answer: Temperature and amount of gas

questions.text: Explain the relationship observed between pressure and volume by referring to the kinetic molecular theory.
questions.topic: Ideal gases and the gas laws
questions.memo_answer:
When volume is decreased
• The same number of gas particles are now occupy a smaller volume.
• Particles collide with each other and walls of the container more frequently.
• More frequent collisions mean greater pressure.
OR
When the volume is increased
• The same number of gas particles are occupy a larger volume.
• Particles collide with each other and walls of the container less frequently.
• Less frequent collisions mean a decrease in pressure.

questions.text: Determine the volume that the gas occupied at 96 kPa.
questions.topic: Ideal gases and the gas laws

questions.text: Calculate the volume occupied by the gas at 252 kPa.
questions.topic: Ideal gases and the gas laws
questions.memo_answer:
(Positive marking from 4.4.)
p1V1 = p2V2
(96)(15,15) = (252)V2
V2 = 5,77 cm³
NOTE: if any other pressure value from the graph is used, no positive marking from 4.4; learners must use the reciprocal value of volume in their substitution.

questions.text: It is observed that the gas does not obey the gas law named in QUESTION 4.1 at very high pressure. Explain this observation.
questions.topic: Ideal gases and the gas laws
questions.memo_answer:
At very high pressure, the volume of the gas particles increases.
At very high pressure the volume of the gas becomes significant and the space inside the container becomes significantly less.
The volume measured is higher than predicted by the ideal gas law

questions.context: QUESTION 5 (Start on a new page.) Consider the balanced equation that shows the decomposition of nitrogen oxide (N2O) into nitrogen (N2) and oxygen (O2) molecules: 2 N2O (g) → 2 N2 (g) + O2 (g). The energy profile graph is drawn for the decomposition of N2O. [Graph of potential energy (kJ·mol⁻¹) against reaction progress: reactants at 164,1 kJ·mol⁻¹, products at 0, with an activation-energy peak between them.]
questions.text: Define the term heat of reaction.
questions.memo_answer: Heat of reaction is the energy absorbed or released per mole in a chemical reaction.

questions.text: Is the above reaction ENDOTHERMIC or EXOTHERMIC? Give a reason for the answer.
questions.memo_answer:
EXOTHERMIC
More energy is released than the energy absorbed.
OR Heat/enthalpy of the products is less than heat/enthalpy of the reactants.
OR ΔH < 0

questions.text: Calculate the heat of reaction.
questions.memo_answer:
ΔH = ΣH(products) - ΣH(reactants)
ΔH = 0 - (164,1)
ΔH = -164,1 kJ·mol⁻¹

questions.text: The energy that is released from the formation of N2 and O2 molecules are 405,30 kJ·mol-1. Calculate the activation energy for this reaction.

Redraw the energy profile graph in your ANSWER BOOK. Draw on the same set of axes the effect that a catalyst would have on the energy profile graph. Indicate the graph of the catalyst with a dotted line.
questions.memo_answer:
Energy profile redrawn (reactants at 164,1 kJ·mol⁻¹, products at 0) with a dotted catalysed curve whose peak is lower than the original peak.
Marking criteria: peak of the catalysed graph is lower; graphs start at the same reactant energy and end horizontally at the same product energy.

questions.context: (Start on a new page.) A certain organic compound (CxHyOz) is composed of 54,54 g of carbon; 9,1 g of hydrogen and 36,36 g of oxygen and has a molecular mass of 88 g·mol-1.
questions.text: Define the term molar mass.
questions.topic: Quantitative aspects: moles, molar volume and concentration
questions.memo_answer: The mass of one mole of a substance. (2 or 0)

questions.text: Determine by calculation, the molecular formula of the organic compound (CxHyOz)
questions.topic: Quantitative aspects: moles, molar volume and concentration
questions.memo_answer:
Marking criteria: (a)-(c) moles of C, H and O; (d) dividing by the smallest number of moles; (e) empirical formula; (f) dividing M(molecular) by M(empirical); (g) correct molecular formula.
n(C) : n(H) : n(O) = 54,54/12 : 9,1/1 : 36,36/16 = 4,545 : 9,100 : 2,2725
Divide by 2,2725: 2 : 4 : 1
Empirical formula: C2H4O
M(C2H4O) = 2(12) + 4(1) + 16 = 44 g·mol⁻¹; n = 88 / 44 = 2
Molecular formula: C4H8O2
questions.memo_note: The guideline prints the carbon mole number as 5,545; 54,54 / 12 = 4,545, which gives the stated ratio 2 : 4 : 1.

questions.context: 6.3 A bottle in a laboratory contains an unknown metal hydroxide (MOH). A lab technician dissolves 1,826 g of the metal hydroxide to make a 100 cm3 solution. Upon analysis it was found that the concentration of the metal hydroxide is 0,326 mol·dm-3.
questions.text: Define the term concentration.
questions.topic: Quantitative aspects: moles, molar volume and concentration
questions.memo_answer: The amount of solute per litre of solution.

questions.text: Determine by calculation, the name of the metal hydroxide.
questions.topic: Quantitative aspects: moles, molar volume and concentration
questions.memo_answer:
n = cV = (0,326)(0,1) = 0,0326 mol
M = m / n = 1,826 / 0,0326 = 56 g·mol⁻¹
M + 16 + 1 = 56, M = 39 g·mol⁻¹ (K)
MOH = potassium hydroxide

questions.context: QUESTION 7 (Start on a new page.) Learners crushed eggshells to determine the percentage of calcium carbonate that are found in a 1,5 g sample. The crushed eggshells are allowed to react with EXCESS hydrochloric acid. The balanced equation for the reaction: CaCO3(s) + 2 HCℓ (aq) → CaCℓ2(aq) + CO2(g) + H2O(ℓ). The calcium carbonate reacted completely in 5 minutes. The graph below shows the carbon dioxide gas that was collected at STP. [Graph: volume of CO2 collected (cm³) against time (minutes); the volume rises to 325 cm³ at 5 minutes and stays constant afterwards.]
questions.text: Define the term limiting reagent.
questions.topic: Quantitative aspects: stoichiometry, limiting reagents and purity
questions.memo_answer: The substance that is completely used up during a chemical reaction.

questions.context: 7.2-7.4 Calculate the:
questions.text: Mass of calcium carbonate contained in the 1,5 g sample of eggshells
questions.topic: Quantitative aspects: stoichiometry, limiting reagents and purity

questions.text: Percentage purity of calcium carbonate in 1,5 g of eggshells
questions.topic: Quantitative aspects: stoichiometry, limiting reagents and purity
questions.memo_answer: % purity = mass CaCO3 / mass of sample x 100 = 1,45 / 1,5 x 100 = 96,67%

questions.text: Number of molecules of HCℓ that reacted with calcium carbonate
questions.topic: Quantitative aspects: stoichiometry, limiting reagents and purity
questions.memo_answer:
CaCO3 : HCℓ = 1 : 2, n(HCℓ) = 2(0,0145) = 0,029 mol
n = N / NA: N = 0,029 x 6,02 x 10²³
N = 1,7458 x 10²² molecules of HCℓ

questions.text: How does the carbon dioxide gas produced after 8 min compare to the carbon dioxide gas produced at 5 min? Write down only HIGHER THAN, SMALLER THAN or EQUAL TO. Give a reason for the answer.
questions.topic: Quantitative aspects: stoichiometry, limiting reagents and purity
questions.memo_answer:
Equal to
After the calcium carbonate has completely reacted (at 5 min) there is no more CO2 produced.

questions.context: QUESTION 8 (Start on a new page.) Consider the reaction below: HSO4⁻ (aq) + H2O (ℓ) → H3O⁺ (aq) + SO4²⁻ (aq)
questions.text: Define an acid in terms of Arrhenius theory.
questions.memo_answer: An acid is a substance that produces hydrogen ions (H⁺)/hydronium ions (H3O⁺) when it dissolves in water.

questions.context: 8.2 From the reaction above, write down the:
questions.text: Formulae of the TWO substances that can act as ampholytes
questions.memo_answer: HSO4⁻ and H2O

questions.text: Conjugate base of HSO4⁻
questions.memo_answer: SO4²⁻

questions.context: 8.3 500 cm3 of NaOH are added to 500 cm3 of HNO3 with a concentration of 0,25 mol·dm-3. The temperature of the reaction mixture rises during the reaction. The pH of the final solution is 2,8. The balanced equation is shown below. NaOH (aq) + HNO3 (aq) → NaNO3 (aq) + H2O(ℓ)
questions.text: Describe the term acid base indicator.
questions.memo_answer: An acid-base indicator is a weak acid, or a weak base, which color changes as the H+ ion concentration or the OH— ion concentration in a solution changes.

questions.text: Write down the colour when bromothymol blue is added to HNO3 solution.
questions.memo_answer: Yellow/Geel

questions.text: Is the reaction above EXOTHERMIC or ENDOTHERMIC? Give a reason for the answer.
questions.memo_answer:
Exothermic
It gives off heat / temperature rises

questions.text: Calculate the concentration of H3O+ in the final solution.
Calculate the initial concentration of NaOH solution.
questions.topic: Quantitative aspects: stoichiometry, limiting reagents and purity
questions.memo_answer:
(Positive marking from 8.3.4.)
n(HNO3) initial = cV = (0,25)(0,5) = 0,125 mol
n(HNO3) excess = cV = (1,58 x 10⁻³)(1) = 1,58 x 10⁻³ mol
n(HNO3) reacted = 0,125 - 1,58 x 10⁻³ = 0,123 mol
NaOH : HNO3 = 1 : 1, n(NaOH) = 0,123 mol
[NaOH] initial = n / V = 0,123 / 0,5 = 0,246 mol·dm⁻³

questions.context: QUESTION 9 (Start on a new page.) A clean piece of aluminium metal strip is placed in a copper sulphate (CuSO4) solution. The reaction was observed again after 2 hours. [Diagram: beaker of blue CuSO4(aq) with an Aℓ(s) strip at the start and after 2 hours.] After 2 hours it was observed that the blue solution turned colourless and the shiny metallic aluminium turned brown. The net ionic balanced equation for the reaction is: 2 Aℓ (s) + 3 Cu²⁺(aq) → 3 Cu (s) + 2 Aℓ³⁺(aq)
questions.text: Explain the term oxidation in terms of oxidation number.
questions.memo_answer: It is a number that shows the number of electrons an atom has gained, lost, or shared in a chemical compound, compared to its elemental state.
questions.memo_note: The guideline answer defines oxidation number rather than oxidation; in terms of oxidation number, oxidation is an increase in oxidation number.

questions.context: 9.2 Write down the chemical symbol of a substance that is …
questions.text: oxidised.
questions.memo_answer: Aℓ

questions.text: the oxidising agent.
questions.memo_answer: Cu²⁺

questions.text: Will the oxidation number of the sulphate ion INCREASE, DECREASE or REMAIN THE SAME during this reaction? Give a reason for the answer.
questions.memo_answer:
REMAIN THE SAME
It is the spectator ion

questions.context: 9.4 Acidified potassium dichromate (K2Cr2O7) is an orange solution due to the presence of the dichromate ions (Cr2O7²⁻).
questions.text: Determine the oxidation number of chromium (Cr) in Cr2O7²⁻.

questions.context: When iron sulphate solution (FeSO4) is added to acidified potassium dichromate (K2Cr2O7) solution, the solution changes colour from orange to green after a few seconds. During this reaction Fe²⁺ ions were oxidised to Fe³⁺ and Cr2O7²⁻ is reduced to Cr³⁺.
questions.text: Will the concentration of the potassium dichromate INCREASE, DECREASE or REMAINS THE SAME as the reaction proceeds? Explain the answer by referring to the relevant half-reaction.
questions.memo_answer:
Decreases
Cr2O7²⁻ + 14H⁺ + 6e⁻ → 2Cr³⁺ + 7H2O
Cr2O7²⁻ is reduced to Cr³⁺.

questions.text: Write down the balance net ionic equation for this reaction.
questions.memo_answer:
Cr2O7²⁻ + 14H⁺ + 6e⁻ → 2Cr³⁺ + 7H2O
6(Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ + e⁻)
Cr2O7²⁻ + 6Fe²⁺ + 14H⁺ → 2Cr³⁺ + 6Fe³⁺ + 7H2O
Marking: balancing electrons by multiplying the oxidation half-reaction by 6 (1); reactants (1); products (1).
